title: India Warns TV Channels on Anti-National Debates, Caps AI to Assistive Role
excerpt: The I&B Ministry's advisory tells private satellite channels to enforce the Programme Code on debates, crime coverage and AI use — or face action under the 1995 Cable Television Act.
body:
• India's I&B Ministry on Wednesday advised private satellite TV channels to strictly follow the Programme Code, warning that violations could invite action under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995.
  • Debates and panel discussions must not "promote or encourage communal or anti-national attitudes"; channels should vet and sensitise panellists and mute, interrupt or cut feeds when remarks turn derogatory or inflammatory.
  • AI tools, including generative AI for graphics and virtual presenters, may be used only in an "assistive capacity" and must not compromise accuracy, authenticity or sensitivity.
  • The advisory also bars live coverage of anti-terror operations, requires time-stamps on disaster visuals, Survey of India maps only, and protection of sexual-offence victims' identities.

India's Ministry of Information and Broadcasting on Wednesday issued an advisory to private satellite television channels, asking them to strictly adhere to the Programme Code and warning that violations could invite regulatory action. The advisory, reported by BestMediaInfo and other outlets, followed a meeting of the ministry's Inter-Departmental Committee, which found telecasts on various channels "not in conformity with the spirit of the Programme Code."

The committee also noted that similar news and visuals were being broadcast across multiple channels on the same subjects, and stressed that inappropriate behaviour or language should not be normalised in telecasts.

What the Advisory Actually Requires

The Programme Code is prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994. The advisory does not create new law; it tells channels the existing code will be enforced. Its specific instructions cover debates, crime and violence coverage, disaster reporting and the use of artificial intelligence.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2112880291463545211

On debates, channels must ensure that live discussions do not promote or encourage communal or anti-national attitudes. That means careful selection and prior sensitisation of panellists, adequate editorial control during the programme, and immediate remedial measures — muting, disclaimers, interruption or discontinuation of the feed — when content turns derogatory, abusive or inflammatory.

"The use of AI tools may be limited to assistive capacity without compromising the accuracy, authenticity or sensitivity of news content."

— Ministry of Information and Broadcasting advisory, October 21, 2026

The AI Rule, in Practice

The AI provision is the advisory's most forward-looking element. Channels may use AI, including generative tools for graphics and virtual news presentations, but only as an assistant: editorial responsibility stays with the broadcaster, and the technology must not distort factual reporting. In practical terms, an AI-generated graphic or a virtual presenter segment that misstates facts would be the channel's violation, not the tool's. The ministry also asked broadcasters to strengthen editorial and content review mechanisms and to sensitise staff across news gathering, editing, production and telecast, encouraging regular workshops on the Programme Code.

The Rest of the List

The advisory reiterates the standing prohibition on live coverage of anti-terror operations, which is restricted to periodic briefings by authorised officers. Visuals of natural disasters and major accidents should be time-stamped wherever necessary to avoid misleading viewers or causing panic, and reports must rest on verified facts rather than unverified, sensationalised crime coverage or excessive replays of violent footage. Channels must use only authentic maps of India published by the Survey of India, in broadcasts, graphics and digital representations alike. They must also protect the identities of victims of sexual offences, in line with Supreme Court directions, withholding photographs, family details and locality information that could identify a victim.

Why It Matters Beyond India

Indian news channels reach diaspora audiences worldwide through satellite and streaming, and their prime-time debates shape political conversation in Indian households abroad. The advisory's enforcement test will be whether monitoring under the existing Act produces visible action against repeat offenders; as Nation Press noted in its summary, further regulatory action is possible if compliance is not demonstrated in subsequent monitoring cycles. No broadcaster or press-freedom organisation response was carried in the initial coverage of the advisory.

What to Watch

Advisories of this kind have been issued before; the open question is follow-through. Channels are expected to demonstrate compliance in upcoming monitoring, and the ministry has signalled that breaches of the Programme Code can draw action under the 1995 Act and its rules. The AI clause, in particular, sets a marker that other regulators wrestling with synthetic media in newsrooms will watch.
